title: Where a max or min search starts
summary: Why a maximum or minimum search can give a wrong answer when its starting value does not come from the data.
objectives: Explain why starting a maximum at `0` fails when every value is negative.
Trace how a running maximum changes during a loop.
Initialize a maximum or minimum from the first array value.
Recognize the same initialization mistake in related searches.

bad.title: Code Coach flags this pattern

good.title: Start with a value from the data

blocks.note: The first version compiles, but its answer is wrong when the loop runs. None of the negative values is greater than `0`, so `max` stays `0`. The largest value in the array is `-2`. The fix is to start with a value that is actually in the array.

blocks.text: A running maximum is a variable that holds the largest value seen so far. The loop compares each new value with that variable. If the starting value is `0`, but every value is negative, no array value can replace it. The loop has no way to know that `0` was not in the array.

blocks.caption: How the wrong starting value blocks every negative temperature
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start with max as zero]) --> B[Read next temperature]
  B --> C{Is temperature greater than max?}
  C -- yes --> D[Replace max with temperature]
  C -- no --> E[Keep max unchanged]
  D --> F{More temperatures?}
  E --> F
  F -- yes --> B
  F -- no --> G([Report max])

blocks.caption: The temperatures and the starting value
blocks.name: temps
blocks.note: The highlighted value, `-2`, is the largest value in `temps`. The starting value `0` is outside the array and is larger than every temperature here.

blocks.title: Compile time or run time?
blocks.text: This is a logic mistake, not a syntax mistake. Java accepts the code at compile time. It does not give a warning about the wrong starting value. The wrong answer appears when the program runs.

sections.title: Trace the loop one value at a time

blocks.text: A trace is a record of what values variables hold as code runs. Follow `max` through the flagged loop. The test `t > max` asks whether the new temperature is larger than the value currently stored in `max`.
The loop checks every temperature, but none can replace `0`. With `max` set to the first temperature, `-4`, the later values can replace it when they are larger. That lets the loop finish with `-2`.

This complete program uses the temperatures from the flagged code. It sets `max` to the first temperature, then compares every temperature with it. This example assumes the array has at least one value.

blocks.title: Why this gives the right result
items: The first temperature, `-4`, is the best value seen so far.
The next value, `-9`, is not greater than `-4`, so `max` stays `-4`.
The last value, `-2`, is greater than `-4`, so `max` becomes `-2`.
The loop ends with the largest value from the array in `max`.

blocks.text: The same idea works for a minimum. Starting `min` at `0` fails when all the data is positive: no positive value is less than `0`. Start with the first value, then replace it whenever a smaller value appears.

blocks.title: Check the direction
blocks.text: For a maximum, replace the saved value when the new value is greater: `t > max`. For a minimum, replace it when the new value is smaller: `score < min`.

The flagged pattern is `int max = 0` when the data can all be below zero. The reverse mistake is starting a minimum at `0` when the data can all be above zero. Both mistakes let a value that is not in the data affect the answer.

bad.title: Wrong minimum start for positive data

good.title: Minimum starts with the first score

blocks.note: The bad version leaves `min` at `0`, even though `0` is not a score. Start from `scores[0]` so the saved minimum is a value from the data.

bad.title: A fixed guess can fail on other data

good.title: Use a value from the array

blocks.note: A fixed starting guess such as `-100` only works if you can be sure every value is at least `-100`. Starting from `values[0]` avoids that guess. This version, like the worked examples, assumes the array is not empty.

blocks.title: What if the array is empty?
blocks.text: An empty array has no first value, so `values[0]` cannot be used. Check that the array has at least one value before starting this kind of search. An empty array needs a separate result or a separate rule.

blocks.question: What does the flagged code leave in `max` after it checks every value?
blocks.explanation: Every temperature is less than `0`, so every test `t > max` is false. The program compiles, but `max` remains `0` when it runs.

blocks.question: Which starting value is suitable for finding the largest value in a non-empty array?
blocks.explanation: `data[0]` is the first value in the array. It gives the loop a real value to compare with the others, even when every value is negative.

blocks.question: You want the smallest value in an array of positive numbers. Which update test and starting value fit that job?
blocks.explanation: Start with a value from the array, then replace it when a smaller value appears. The test `value < min` moves the saved value toward the minimum.

items: The flagged `int max = 0` can compile and still produce a wrong result when all values are negative.
A running maximum or minimum stores the best value seen so far.
For a non-empty array, start a maximum or minimum search with the first element, such as `int max = values[0];`.
For a maximum, update when the new value is greater. For a minimum, update when the new value is smaller.
Starting from the first element assumes the array is not empty, so handle an empty array separately.
